profile.reading:
This building at 1707 West Creek Lane in Chaska, a Minneapolis suburb in Carver County roughly twenty five miles southwest of downtown, is identified as a data center operated by UnitedHealth Group, the Minnetonka, Minnesota based health care company that is among the largest corporations in the United States by revenue. UnitedHealth Group operates through two main businesses. UnitedHealthcare provides health benefit plans to employers, individuals, and government programs including Medicare and Medicaid, while Optum, a health services arm, spans pharmacy benefit management, care delivery, and health technology and data analytics.

A company of that size and structure depends on enormous, continuously operating data infrastructure. Processing health insurance claims, administering pharmacy benefits, running provider networks, and supporting Optum's technology and analytics businesses all require data systems that handle protected health information, which under federal HIPAA law carries strict requirements for security, access control, and auditability. Enterprise data centers supporting that kind of regulated healthcare data are typically built and operated privately by the company itself rather than through a commercial colocation provider, both for direct control over compliance and because a company of UnitedHealth Group's scale can support the capital cost of owned infrastructure more efficiently than leasing it.

Chaska sits within the broader Minneapolis Saint Paul metropolitan area, a region UnitedHealth Group and its predecessor companies have called home since the company's founding in Minnetonka in the 1970s, and Carver County has seen substantial suburban office and light industrial development over the past two decades as Twin Cities area companies expanded outside the urban core. No public filing, press release, or trade coverage describing this specific building's square footage, power capacity, staffing, or construction date could be located, and UnitedHealth Group's own investor and corporate communications materials do not name individual data center sites. That absence of published detail is standard practice for a private enterprise data center supporting internal healthcare data systems. Unlike a commercial data center operator marketing capacity to tenants, a company running its own regulated infrastructure has every incentive to keep its physical security posture, exact capacity, and operational specifics out of public view, disclosing only what zoning, permitting, or tax assessment processes require at the county level.
